entries.title: Does policy evaluation depend on the quality of democracy?
entries.abstract: Policy evaluation contributes to the quality of democracy, but does the quality of democracy, in turn, contribute to the production and use of policy evaluation? Existing research provides evidence for the former claim but not for the latter. Addressing this research gap, this article examines the pertinence of democratic characteristics alongside or in combination with economic, bureaucratic and educational capacities and analyses the extent to which they are necessary or sufficient for the production and use of policy evaluation. Drawing on Bertelsmann’s Sustainable Governance Indicators (SGI), the analysis applies fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to all 41 OECD and EU countries. entries.title: The politics of policy transfer: political dynamics in OECD accession
entries.abstract: While recent scholarship has called for greater attention to the political dynamics of policy transfer, this dimension remains under-theorised in policy studies. Existing work has convincingly shown that transfer is politically motivated yet often lacks analytical tools capable of systematically unpacking these dynamics. Drawing on political sociology, it conceptualises policy transfer as a process of mobilisation by interested actors occupying positions within organisational fields. entries.title: Explaining policy stasis on same-sex unions in Peru
entries.abstract: This article advances understanding of how policy monopolies sustain policy stasis in morality policy, where scholarship has explained policy change more fully than its absence. It develops the concept of a moral policy monopoly to examine how interlocking mechanisms can sustain policy stasis in contexts of high religiosity. entries.abstract: Abstract Administrative burden scholarship has identified psychological costs alongside learning and compliance costs, yet the category remains homogeneous, grouping stigma, diminished autonomy, and stress, without a shared organizing principle. This article advances a mechanism-level account centered on recognition, drawing on a qualitative case study of claiming disability benefits in Israel, based on in-depth interviews with 33 individuals (16 young adults with diagnosed mental health conditions and 17 social and outreach workers). entries.title: Why policy actors choose not to coordinate in policy conflicts
entries.abstract: Research on advocacy coalitions in public policy highlights the importance of coordination among policy actors seeking to influence policy making. Less attention has been devoted to why actors sometimes choose not to coordinate, even when they share similar beliefs or interests. In this study, we explore the rationales behind actors’ decisions to refrain from publicly visible coordination in wind power development projects in two Swedish municipalities over a 16-year period. Our findings show that, while most actors engage in coordination at some point, they also refrain from coordinating with others for several reasons.
